title: Vitamin D supplementation for prevention of mortality in adults
authors: Bjelakovic G, Gluud LL, Nikolova D, Whitfield K, Wetterslev J, Simonetti RG, et al.
followUp: weighted mean 4.4 years of vitamin D administration
population: 56 randomised trials with usable mortality data, all in high-income countries; most included women older than 70 years (mean proportion of women 77%); 35 trials in older people living independently or in institutional care; searches to February 2012
funder: Internal: The Copenhagen Trial Unit, Centre for Clinical Intervention Research, Rigshospitalet, Denmark. External: Ministry of Science, Republic of Serbia. No statement on the role of the funders was found.
result: All forms of vitamin D: deaths 5,920 of 47,472 (12.5%) against 6,077 of 47,814 (12.7%), RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.94 to 0.99); more than 8% of participants dropped out, and worst-best and best-worst case analyses showed that vitamin D could be associated with a dramatic increase or decrease in mortality. Vitamin D3: 4,153 of 37,817 (11.0%) against 4,340 of 38,110 (11.4%), RR 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98; 38 trials), about 150 people treated for 5 years per death prevented; vitamin D2, alfacalcidol and calcitriol did not significantly affect mortality. No significant subgroup differences, including baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D below against at or above 20 ng/mL, ambulatory against institutionalised, and with or without calcium. Vitamin D3 decreased cancer mortality, RR 0.88 (0.78 to 0.98; 4 trials, 44,492). Vitamin D3 combined with calcium increased nephrolithiasis, RR 1.17 (1.02 to 1.34; 4 trials, 42,876). Alfacalcidol and calcitriol increased hypercalcaemia, RR 3.18 (1.17 to 8.68; 3 trials, 710).
